question: How does object-oriented programming work in JavaScript compared to classical OOP languages?
shortAnswer: JS is prototype-based; ES6 classes are syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototypes, with some semantic differences (e.g. non-callable without `new`).
detailedAnswer: Instead of class-copy inheritance (classical), JS links objects via prototypes. You can still model encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism. `class` syntax provides constructors, `extends`, `super`, static members, and private fields (`#`), but underneath instances still delegate to prototypes. Objects are dynamic: properties can be added at runtime. Mixins and composition are idiomatic alternatives to deep hierarchies. Interviewers often want you to acknowledge both the prototype model and modern class ergonomics.
interviewTip: Say 'prototype-based with class sugar' — concise and accurate.
commonMistake: Claiming JS had no OOP before `class`.

question: Explain `extends` and `super` in JavaScript classes. What must a derived constructor do before using `this`?
shortAnswer: `extends` sets up prototype linkage; derived constructors must call `super()` before accessing `this` so the parent can initialize the instance.
detailedAnswer: `class Child extends Parent` makes `Child.prototype` delegate to `Parent.prototype` and sets `Child.[[Prototype]]` to `Parent` for static inheritance. In the child constructor, `super(args)` invokes the parent constructor with the current `new.target`. Until `super` returns, `this` is uninitialized in the derived constructor — accessing it throws. `super.method()` in a method calls the parent prototype's method with the same `this`. Arrow fields are not on the prototype, so `super` patterns differ. Returning an object from a constructor still overrides the instance.
interviewTip: Mention static inheritance via `extends` — often overlooked.
commonMistake: Using `this` before `super()` in a subclass constructor.

question: When would you choose composition over inheritance in a JavaScript codebase?
shortAnswer: Prefer composition when behavior is reusable across unrelated types or hierarchies would be deep/fragile; use inheritance for true 'is-a' with shared identity.
detailedAnswer: Inheritance couples types: changes in a base class ripple downward (fragile base class). Composition (`has-a`) plugs small collaborators into a host object/function, easing testing and reuse. In JS, composition is natural via closures, dependency injection, and mixins — but mixins can conflict. Use inheritance for framework extension points (`extends Component`) or clear taxonomic relationships. A practical heuristic: if you only need a few methods, wrap or delegate; if you need polymorphism with shared interface and lifecycle, inheritance or explicit interfaces (TypeScript) may fit.
interviewTip: Give one concrete domain example (e.g. payment processors vs shared BaseManager god class).
commonMistake: Dogmatically banning inheritance even for genuine framework subclassing.

question: Compare ES private class fields (`#`) with WeakMap-based privacy patterns.
shortAnswer: `#fields` are language-enforced per-class privacy; WeakMaps associate hidden data with objects without exposing properties — useful for wrapping external objects.
detailedAnswer: Private fields are only accessible inside the class body (including its methods); access from outside throws. They are not inherited as accessible names in subclasses (subclasses declare their own `#`). WeakMap privacy stores values keyed by the instance; if you don't export the map, data is effectively private and entries don't prevent GC. WeakMaps can decorate objects you don't control (e.g. DOM nodes). Trade-offs: `#` is clearer and faster in engines for typical class design; WeakMap is more flexible for libraries that attach metadata. Neither is a security boundary across realms.
interviewTip: Discuss GC friendliness of WeakMap — senior detail.
commonMistake: Using a module-level plain Map keyed by instance and leaking memory after instances die.

question: You are leading a redesign of a large JS domain layer that mixed anemic data objects with scattered business rules. How would you structure OOP (or FP) boundaries?
shortAnswer: Define clear domain entities/services with invariants in one place; keep infrastructure (HTTP/DB/UI) outside; prefer small composable types over deep class trees.
detailedAnswer: Start by identifying bounded contexts and ubiquitous language. Model invariants on entities/value objects (classes or factories that validate on construction). Put use-cases in application services that orchestrate domain objects — avoid UI components owning rules. Prefer composition of policies/strategies over a mega-base `Entity`. Decide immutability defaults for value objects. For JS/TS, TypeScript interfaces + modules often beat deep inheritance. Establish testing strategy: pure domain unit tests without DOM/network. Migration: strangler-fig new modules beside legacy anemic models; forbid new business logic in controllers. Measure success by reduced duplication and fewer cross-layer leaks.
interviewTip: Talk migration and team conventions, not only UML.
commonMistake: Rewriting everything into a textbook GoF pattern catalog without incremental delivery.
